\section{Hypercontractivity --- Random Variables --- Discrete}

\subsection*{Hypercontractivity --- Random Variables --- Discrete: Introduction}
Minimum atom mass controls higher norms and gives affine hypercontractive radii for centered and symmetric finite laws. The sharp radius is attained by a centered two-point law and characterizes its possible contractions.

\subsection*{Hypercontractivity --- Random Variables --- Discrete: Results}

\begin{theorem}[Higher Norm from Minimum Atom Mass]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.discrete_lp_norm_le}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.HasAtomLowerBound, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.rvLpNorm}
\difficulty{6}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be measurable.
Suppose $X$ is supported almost everywhere on a finite set whose points each have
probability at least $\lambda$, and let $q>2$ and $\lambda>0$. Then the real-valued
extended-norm conversion specified by $N_r(X)=(\|X\|_{L^r(\mu)})_{\mathbb R}$ satisfies
$N_q(X)\le (1/\lambda)^{1/2-1/q}N_2(X)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Discrete Centered Hypercontractivity]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.discrete_hypercontractive}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.HasAtomLowerBound, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.HasAtomLowerBound.memLp, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.conjugate, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.const_mul, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.mono_radius, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.discrete_lp_norm_le, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.mean_zero_hypercontractive, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.rvLpNorm}
\difficulty{6}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space, let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
mean zero, and suppose there is a finite set supporting $X$ almost everywhere such that
every point in that set has probability at least $\lambda$. If $q>2$ and
$0<\lambda\le1$, set $\rho=\lambda^{1/2-1/q}/(2\sqrt{q-1})$. Then $X$ is affine
hypercontractive both from exponent $2$ to exponent $q$ with parameter $\rho$, and from
exponent $q/(q-1)$ to exponent $2$ with parameter $\rho$: in each case the exponents
satisfy the required order, $0\le\rho<1$, $X$ belongs to the target $L^q$ space, and
$\|a+\rho bX\|_{\text{target}}\le\|a+bX\|_{\text{source}}$ for all real $a,b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Hypercontractivity for symmetric discrete laws]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.symmetric_discrete_hypercontractive}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.HasAtomLowerBound, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.HasAtomLowerBound.memLp, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.conjugate, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.const_mul, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.mono_radius, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsSymmetricRV, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.discrete_lp_norm_le, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.rvLpNorm, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.symmetric_hypercontractive}
\difficulty{6}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be measurable
and symmetric in distribution, with a finite set of values supporting $X$ almost
everywhere and each value in that set having probability at least $\lambda$. Suppose
$q>2$ and $0<\lambda\le1$, and put $\rho=\lambda^{1/2-1/q}/\sqrt{q-1}$. Then $X$ is
$(2,\mathrm{ENNReal}(q),\rho)$-hypercontractive and
$(\mathrm{ENNReal}(q/(q-1)),2,\rho)$-hypercontractive; here hypercontractivity includes
the exponent and parameter constraints, the required integrability, and the affine norm
inequality for every pair of real scalars.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp hypercontractivity for finite laws]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.sharp_discrete_hypercontractive}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.HasAtomLowerBound, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.conjugate, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.SharpDiscrete.finite_law_sharp_forward, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.sharpDiscreteRadius}
\difficulty{3}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space, and let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be
measurable with mean zero. Suppose $q>2$, $0<\lambda<1/2$, and there is a finite set
supporting $X$ almost surely such that each of its points has probability at least
$\lambda$. Set $\rho=\sqrt{\sinh(u/q)/\sinh(u/(q/(q-1)))}$, where
$u=\log((1-\lambda)/\lambda)$. Then for every $a,b\in\mathbb R$, the $L^q$ norm of
$a+\rho bX$ is at most the $L^2$ norm of $a+bX$, and the $L^2$ norm of $a+\rho bX$ is
at most the $L^{q/(q-1)}$ norm of $a+bX$; in both cases $X$ belongs to the output
exponent's $L^p$ space, and the exponents satisfy $1\le p\le q$ with $0\le\rho<1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Optimal radius for a two-point law]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.sharp_discrete_radius_optimal}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.FiniteLaw.centered_two_point_moments, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.conjugate, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.IsHypercontractive.mono_radius, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.SharpDiscrete.two_point_conjugate_radius_le, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.SharpDiscrete.two_point_conjugate_sharp, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.SharpDiscrete.two_point_forward_sharp, BooleanAnalysis.Hypercontractivity.sharpDiscreteRadius}
\difficulty{4}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space, let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be
measurable, and suppose $q>2$, $0<\lambda<1/2$, and $0\le\rho<1$. Assume
$\mu(X=1-\lambda)=\lambda$ and $\mu(X=-\lambda)=1-\lambda$. Set
$u=\log((1-\lambda)/\lambda)$ and $\rho_*=\sqrt{\sinh(u/q)/\sinh(u/(q/(q-1)))}$.
Then the inequality $\|a+\rho bX\|_q\le\|a+bX\|_2$ holds for all real $a,b$ if and
only if $\rho\le\rho_*$; likewise, $\|a+\rho bX\|_2\le\|a+bX\|_{q/(q-1)}$ holds
for all real $a,b$ if and only if $\rho\le\rho_*$.
\end{theorem}
